The lasso’s exact zero coefficients arise from finding the model of a nondifferentiable posterior density. A continuous Laplace prior itself does not assign positive probability to the event \(\beta_j=0\).
The estimator’s nonlinear and nondifferentiable behavior also complicates uncertainty quantification. The estimated active set can change across repeated samples, making OLS standard errors inappropriate if they ignore the selection process.
Tibshirani (1996) considers bootstrap procedures in which the tuning parameter is either held fixed or re-estimated in each bootstrap sample. Re-estimating the parameter incorporates an additional source of variability and can produce larger uncertainty estimates.
A local weighted-ridge approximation can also be used to construct an approximate covariance expression
\[
\widehat{\Cov}(\hat \beta) \approx \hat \sigma^2(X^\top  X + \lambda W^\dagger)^{-1} X^\top X (X^\top X +\lambda W^\dagger)^{-1}
\]
However, this approximation may assign zero estimated variance to coefficients that the lasso sets to zero, even though substantial uncertainty may remain about whether the underlying effects are actually absent.
The empirical results in Tibshirani (1996) also demonstrate that no regularization method uniformly dominates the others. When few predictors have strong effects, subset selection or lasso can perform well. When many predictors have moderate effects, the lasso can offer a favorable compromise between shrinkage and selection. When the true model contains many small zero nonzero effects, ridge regression can be preferable because it retains information distributed across many variables.
The \(L_1\) principle can also be extended beyond Gaussian linear regression. For a model with log-likelihood \(\ell(\beta)\), the corresponding penalized estimator is
\[
\hat \beta = \arg\max_\beta \{\ell(\beta) - \lambda ||\beta||_1\}
\]
This provides extensions to generalized linear models and survival regression. Related sparse penalties can be applied to basis expensions, regression trees, and other statistical structures.
The retrospective discussion in Tibshirani (2011) describes further developments, including group lasso, fused lasso, adaptive lasso, graphical lasso, sparse matrix estimation, and related methods. These extensions modify which quantities are penalized while preserving the idea that a nonsmooth penalty can encode structural simplicity.
Nevertheless, an important limitation remains. When several predictors are strongly correlated, the lasso may select one and discard the others. This can produce a sparse model, but the selected variables may be unstable or fail to reveal the underlying group structure.

title: 10  Lasso Regression
section: 4 Elastic Net: Sparsity with Correlated Predictors
text:
4 Elastic Net: Sparsity with Correlated Predictors

4.1 Motivation and the naive elastic net
Consider a regression problem with \(p\) predictors and \(n\) observations, where \(p\) may be much larger than \(n\). Suppose several predictors are strongly correlated because they measure related aspects of the same underlying phenomenon.
The lasso can produce sparse estimates in this setting, but it has two limitations of particular interest. First, it has a sparse solution with at most \(\rank(X)\) active predictors. Second, when several predictors are highly correlated, it may select one representative without retaining the remaining members of the group.
This behavior is undesirable when the group itself carries scientific meaning. In gene-expression analysis, for example, several genes belonging to a related biological process may have highly correlated expression measurements. Identifying only one gene may conceal the broader structure that explains the response.
Ridge regression behaves differently. Because the squared \(L_2\)-penalty is strictly convex, it discourages assigning a share effect entirely to one variable when several correlation variables can represent the same information. The goal is to combine the sparse behavior of the lasso with ridge regression’s tendency to distribute effects among correlated predictors.
Zou and Hastie (2005) begin with the following criterion.

Definition 2 (Naive elastic net) For \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2 \geq 0\), define
\[
L(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \beta) = ||y-X\beta||_2^2 + \lambda_2 ||\beta||_2^2 + \lambda_1 ||\beta||_1
\tag{3}\]
The naive elastic net estimator is
\[
\hat \beta^{\text{naive}} = \arg\min_\beta L(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \beta).
\]

Here, \(\lambda_1\) controls the \(L_1\)-penalty responsible for sparsity, while \(\lambda_2\) controls the quadratic penalty that stabilizes the coefficients.
For \(\lambda_1+ \lambda_2>0\), let \(\alpha = \frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}\). Then, up to an overall positive scaling factor, the penalty can be written as
\[
J_{\alpha}(\beta) = (1-\alpha)||\beta||_1 + \alpha||\beta||_2^2
\]
This is the mixing convention using in Zou and Hastie (2005): \(\alpha=0\) corresponds to the lasso penalty and \(\alpha=1\) to the ridge penalty. Some modern software packages use the opposite interpretation of their mixing parameter.
For \(0< \alpha< 1\), the penalty is nondifferentiable whenever a coordiante is zero, owing to the \(L_1\)-component, and strictly convex because of the positive quadratic component. Strict convexity improves uniqueness and stability, while nondifferentiability permits exact zeros.


View Python code
import numpy as np 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt 

b = np.linspace(-1.5, 1.5, 400)
B1, B2 = np.meshgrid(b, b)

l1 = np.abs(B1) + np.abs(B2)
l2 = B1**2 + B2**2
enet = 0.5*l1 + 0.5*l2 

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize = (11, 4)) 

for ax, penalty, title in zip(axes, [l1, l2, enet], ["Lasso (L1)", "Ridge (L2)", "Elastic Net"]):
    ax.contour(B1, B2, penalty, levels=[1])
    ax.axhline(0, lw=0.5, color="gray")
    ax.axvline(0, lw=0.5, color="gray")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlim(-1.5, 1.5)
    ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 1.5)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The lasso contraint has sharp vertices on the coordinate axes, while the ridge constraint has a smooth curved boundary. The elastic net combines both characteristic; it retains axis-aligned corners associated with sparsity but introduces curvature away from the axes.


4.2 The augmented-data repersentation
A useful property of the naive elastic net is that its optimization problem can be transformed into a lasso problem on an augmented dataset.

Lemma 1 (Augmented-data equivalence) Given \(y, X\), and fixed \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2\), define
\[
X^* = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\lambda_2}}\begin{pmatrix}X \\ \sqrt{\lambda_2} I_p \end{pmatrix},\quad  y^* = \begin{pmatrix}y \\ 0_p\end{pmatrix}
\]
Let \[
\beta^* = \sqrt{1+ \lambda_2}\beta, \quad \gamma = \frac{\lambda_1}{\sqrt{1+ \lambda_2}}
\]
Then the naive elastic net criterion is exactly equivalent to
\[
L^*(\gamma, \beta^*) = ||y^* - X^* \beta^*||_2^2 + \gamma||\beta^*||_1.
\]
If \(\hat \beta^*\) solves the augmented lasso problem, then
\[
\hat \beta^\text{naive} = \frac{\hat \beta^*}{\sqrt{1+ \lambda_2}}
\]


Proof. Substitute the augmented matrices
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|y^* - X^* \beta ^*\|_2^2 &= \left\|\begin{pmatrix}y \\ 0\end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+ \lambda_2}}\begin{pmatrix}X \\ \sqrt{\lambda_2}I\end{pmatrix}\beta^* \right\|_2^2 \\
&= \left\| y - \frac{X\beta^*}{\sqrt{1+\lambda_2}}\right\|_2^2 + \left\|\frac{\sqrt{\lambda_2} \beta^*}{\sqrt{1+ \lambda_2}}\right\|
\end{aligned}
\]
Using \(\beta^* = \sqrt{1+\lambda_2}\beta\),
\[
\| y^* - X^*\beta^* \|_2^2 = \|y- X\beta \|_2^2 + \lambda_2 \|\beta\|_2^2
\]
Similarly,
\[
\gamma\|\beta^*\|_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\lambda_2}}\sqrt{1+\lambda_2} ||\beta||_1 = \lambda_1 \|\beta\|_1
\]
Thus,
\[
L^*(\gamma, \beta^*) = \|y - X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda_2\|\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda_1 \|\beta\|_1,
\]
which is exactly the naive elastic net criterion. The transformation is invertible, so the minimizers correspond as stated.

The augmented design matrix has \(n+ p\) rows and \(p\) columns, with
\[
{X^*}^{\top}X^* = \frac{X^\top X + \lambda_2 I}{1+ \lambda_2}.
\]
If \(\lambda_2>0\), this matrix is positive definite, even when \(X^\top X\) is singular. Therefore, the augmented problem has a full-column-rank design matrix. The naive elastic net can potentially select all \(p\) predictors, rather than being constrained to a sparse representation with at most \(n\) active predictors.


4.3 Orthonormal elastic net and double shrinkage
Under an orthonomal design, \(x^\top X= I\), the naive elastic net objective separates across coordinates just as the lasso objective does. For a single coefficient,
\[
(\beta_j - \hat \beta_j^{\text{OLS}})^2 + \lambda_2\beta_j^2 + \lambda_1 |\beta_j|
\]
is minimized.

Proposition 5 (Orthonormal naive elastic net) If \(X^\top X = I_p,\) then
\[
\hat \beta_j^{\text{naive}} = \frac{S(\hat \beta_j^\text{OLS}, \lambda_1/2)}{1 + \lambda_2}
\]


Proof. Ignoring constants, the scalar objective is
\[
(1+ \lambda_2)\beta_j^2 -2\hat \beta_j^\text{OLS} \beta_j + \lambda_1 |\beta_j|
\]
For \(\beta_j>0\), the first order-condition is
\[
2(1+\lambda_2)\beta_j - 2\hat \beta_j^{\text{OLS}} + \lambda_1 = 0,
\]
giving
\[
\beta_j = \frac{\hat \beta_j^{\text{OLS}} - \lambda_1 / 2}{1+ \lambda_2}
\]
For \(\beta_j < 0\), the corresponding expression is
\[
\beta_j = \frac{\hat \beta_j^{\text{OLS}} + \lambda_1 / 2}{1+ \lambda_2}
\]
At zero, the subgradient condition requires
\[
|\hat \beta_j^{\text{OLS}} |\leq \lambda_1 / 2
\]
Combining the three cases gives the claimed result.

The \(L_1\) component first substracts a threshold and potentially sets the coefficient to zero. The quadratic component the scales the remaining coefficient by \(1/(1+\lambda_2)\).
This can create excessive shrinkage. Once the lasso component has already reduced the coefficient magnitude, the additional scaling may introduce more bias than is beneficial for prediction. Zou and Hastie (2005) therefore distinguish the naive elastic net from a corrected estimator, which will be developed after establishing the grouping effect.


4.4 The grouping effect
A central motivation for the elastic net is its tendency to assign similar coefficients to strongly correlated predictors.
A regression method exhibits a grouping effect when variables with highly correlated predictor columns tend to receive similar estimated coefficients, up to a sign change for negatively correlated variables. The extreme case occurs when two predictor columns are identical, i.e., \(x_i = x_j\). These predictors contain the same information about the response.
Consider the general problem
\[
\hat \beta = \arg\min_\beta \{\| y - X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda J(\beta)\}, \quad \lambda > 0
\]

Lemma 2 (Identical predictors) Suppose \(x_i = x_j\). If \(J\) is strictly convex and invariant under exchanging coordinates \(i\) and \(j\), then \(\hat \beta_i = \hat \beta_j\). for the lasso penalty \(J(\beta) = \|\beta\|_1\), the optimal coefficients have
\[
\hat \beta_i \hat \beta_j \geq 0,
\]
but need not be equal. If \(\hat \beta\) is a minimizer, then replacing the two coefficients by
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tilde{\beta_i} &= s(\hat \beta_i + \hat \beta_j),\\
\tilde{\beta_j} &= (1-s)(\hat \beta_i + \hat \beta_j), \quad 0 \leq s\leq 1,  
\end{aligned}
\]
produces another minimizer.


Proof. Suppose first that \(J\) is strictly convex and symmetric in the two coordinates. Let \(\tilde{\beta}\) be obtained by exchanging \(\hat \beta_i\) and \(\hat \beta_j\). Since \(x_i = x_j\),
\[
X\tilde{\beta} = X\hat \beta
\]
Symmetry gives \(J(\tilde{\beta}) = J(\hat \beta)\), so \(\tilde{\beta}\) is also a minimizer. If \(\hat \beta_i \neq \hat \beta_j\), then \(\hat \beta \neq \tilde{\beta}\). Strict convexity implies
\[
J\left(\frac{\hat \beta + \tilde \beta}{2}\right) < \frac{J(\hat \beta) + J(\tilde{\beta})}{2}
\]
The midpoint has exactly the same fitted values as the two original vectors, so its objective is strictly smaller. This contradicts optimality. Thus \(\hat \beta_i = \hat \beta_j\)
For the lasso, suppose that \(\hat \beta_i\) and \(\hat \beta_j\) have opposite signs. Then
\[
|\hat \beta_i + \hat \beta_j| < |\hat \beta_i| + |\hat \beta_j|
\]
Combining their contributiosn into a single coefficeint leaves \(X\hat\beta\) unchanged but strictly reduces the \(L_1\)-penalty. This is impossible at an optinum, so the two coefficients must have the same sign or one must be zero. When this condition holds,
\[
|\hat \beta_i| + |\hat \beta_j| = |\hat \beta_i + \hat \beta_j|
\]
Any redistribution of their sum using the stated nonnegative proportions preserves the fitted values and the penalty, producing another minimizer.

For the elastic net, strict convexity guarantees equal coefficients when two predictor columns are identical. For the lasso, the estimated coefficients need not be unique, even though the combined fitted effect is determined.
The grouping effect can also be quantified when predictor columns are close but not identical.

Theorem 4 (Quantitative grouping effect) Assume the response is centered, the predictors satisfy \(\|x_j \|_2= 1\), and \(\lambda_2 > 0\). Let \(\hat \beta(\lambda_1, \lambda_2)\) denote the naive elastic net estimate. Suppose
\[
\hat \beta_i \hat \beta_j > 0.
\]
Define
\[
D_{\lambda_1, \lambda_2}(i, j) = \frac{|\hat \beta_i - \hat \beta_j|}{\|y\|_2}
\]
for \(y\neq 0\), and let \(\rho = x_i^\top x_j\). Then
\[
D_{\lambda_1, \lambda_2}(i, j) \leq \frac{\sqrt{2(1-p)}}{\lambda_2}
\]


Proof. The two coefficients are nonzero and have the same sign. Therefore, the differentiable first-order conditions for the active coordinates are
\[
-2x_i^\top r + \lambda_1 \mathrm{sign}(\hat \beta_i) + 2\lambda_2 \hat \beta_i = 0
\]
and
\[
-2x_j^\top r + \lambda_1 \mathrm{sign}(\hat \beta_j) + 2\lambda_2 \hat \beta_j = 0
\]
where \(r= y - X\hat \beta\). Since the signs are equal, the \(L_1\)-penalty terms cancel when the equations are subtracted. Hence
\[
\lambda_2(\hat \beta_i - \hat \beta_j) = (x_i - x_j)^\top r
\]
Taking absolute values and applying Cauchy-Schwarz,
\[
|\hat \beta_i - \hat \beta_j| \leq \frac{\|x_i - x_j\|_2 \|r\|_2}{\lambda_2}
\]
By optimality,
\[
L(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \hat \beta) \leq L(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, 0) = \|y\|_2^2
\]
Because the penalty terms are nonnegative,
\[
\|r\|_2 \leq \|y \|_2
\]
Also,
\[
\|x_i - x_j \|_2^2 = \|x_i\|^2_2 + \|x_j\|_2^2 -2x_i^\top x_j = 2(1-\rho)
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{|\hat \beta_i -\hat \beta_j|}{\|y\|_2} \leq \frac{\sqrt{2(1-p)}}{\lambda_2}
\]

If two positively correlated predictors have nonzero coefficients of the same sign, the difference between their estimated coefficients is bounded by a quantity approaching zero as \(\rho \to 1\).
The lasso, corresponding to \(\lambda_2=0\) does not possess this bound. The theorem is proved for the naive estimator; after the original elastic net rescaling, the coefficient difference and its upper bound are both multiplied by \(1+ \lambda_2\).


View Python code
import numpy as np 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt 

def soft(z, t): 
    return np.sign(z) * max(abs(z) - t, 0)

def fit(X, y , lam1, lam2=0, iterations=5000):
    beta = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(iterations):
        old = beta.copy()
        for j in range(X.shape[1]):
            r = y - X@beta + X[:, j] * beta[j]
            beta[j] = soft(X[:, j] @ r, lam1/2) / (X[:, j] @ X[:, j] + lam2)
            if np.max(abs(beta-old)) < 1e-10:
                break
    return beta 

rng = np.random.default_rng(6400)
u, v = rng.normal(size=(2, 100))

u -= u.mean()
u /= np.linalg.norm(u)

v -= v.mean() 
v -= u @ v * u 
v /= np.linalg.norm(v) 

y = 3*u + 0.1* v 
rhos = np.linspace(0, 0.999, 60)

lasso_coef, enet_coef = [] , []
lam1, lam2 = 0.35, 0.75 

for rho in rhos: 
    x1 = u
    x2 = rho*u + np.sqrt(1-rho**2)*v
    X = np.column_stack([x1, x2])

    lasso_coef.append(fit(X, y, lam1))
    naive = fit(X, y, lam1, lam2)
    enet_coef.append((1+ lam2) * naive)

lasso_coef = np.array(lasso_coef)
enet_coef = np.array(enet_coef)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))

for ax, coef, title in zip(axes, [lasso_coef, enet_coef], ["Lasso", "Corrected elastic net"]):
    ax.plot(rhos, coef[:, 0], label=r"$\beta_1$")
    ax.plot(rhos, coef[:, 1], label=r"$\beta_2$")
    ax.set(xlabel="Correlation between predictors", ylabel="Estimated coefficient", title=title)
    ax.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









When two predictors become nearly identical, the lasso can allocate most of their shared effect to one coefficient. The elastic net’s quadratic component encourages the two estimates to approach one another. The precise paths depend on the response and penalty parameters. The theorem guarantees closeness for the naive elastic net under its stated assumptions; it does not assert that every correlated group must enter the model together in every dataset.

title: 10  Lasso Regression
section: 5 The corrected elastic net: stabilization without excessive shrinkage
text:
5 The corrected elastic net: stabilization without excessive shrinkage

5.1 Correcting the naive elastic net
The naive elastic net combines the advantages of the \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) penalties, but its orthonormal solution reveals a problem:
\[
\hat \beta_j^\text{naive} = \frac{S(\hat \beta_j^\text{OLS}, \lambda_1/2)}{1+ \lambda_2}
\]
The \(L_1\)-component already shrinks the coefficient through soft thresholding. The quadratic component then applies an additional multiplicative reduction. Although both shrinkage mechanisms can reduce variance, their combined effect may introduce unnecessary bias. The naive elastic net can therefore perform poorly in prediction even when its variable selection and grouping behavior are desirable. To address this, Zou and Hastie (2005) introduce a corrected estimator by rescaling the naive elastic net coefficients.

Definition 3 (Corrected elastic net) Let \(\hat \beta^{\text{naive}}\) minimize Equation 3. The corrected elastic net estimator is defined as
\[
\hat \beta^{\text{EN}} = (1+\lambda_2)\hat\beta^{\text{naive}}
\]

Equivalently, from the augmented-data representation,
\[
\hat \beta^{\text{EN}} = \sqrt{1+ \lambda_2} \hat \beta^*.
\]
The rescaling is a positive scalar transformation, so it does not change which coefficients are zero. Therefore,
\[
\hat \beta_j^\text{EN} = 0 \Longleftrightarrow \hat \beta_j^\text{naive} = 0
\]
The selected variables and their coefficient signs remain unchanged, while the magnitudes of the nonzero coefficients increase. This means that the corrected estimator retains the sparsity and grouping properties of the naive elastic net while compensating for its additional shrinkage.

Proposition 6 (Orthonormal corrected elastic net) If \(X^\top X = I_p\), then
\[
\hat \beta_j^{\text{EN}} = S(\hat \beta_j^\text{OLS}, \lambda_1/2)
\]


Proof. From Proposition 5,
\[
\hat\beta_j^\text{naive} = \frac{S(\hat \beta_j^{\text{OLS}}, \lambda_1/2)}{1+\lambda_2}
\]
Applying the corrected estimator definition gives
\[
\hat \beta_j^\text{EN} = (1+\lambda_2)\hat \beta_j^\text{naive} = S(\hat \beta_j^\text{OLS}, \lambda_1/2)
\]

When predictors are orthogonal, there is no multicolinearity to stabilize, and the corrected elastic net reduces to the lasso. Thus, the direct scaling effect of the quadratic penalty has been removed.
When predictors are correlated, however, the quadratic penalty still changes the way coeffcients are jointly estimated. The corrected elastic net consequently retains the stabilization effect of ridge regularization without imposing the same additional coefficient scaling.


5.2 Elastic net as a stabilized zero
The rescaling has a deeper mathematical interpretation. It can be expressed as a modification of the quadratic component of the lasso objective of the lasso objective.

Theorem 5 (Stabilized quadratic representation) The corrected elastic net estimator satisfies
\[
\hat \beta^{EN} = \arg\min_\beta \left\{ \beta^\top \left(\frac{X^\top X + \lambda_2 I}{1 + \lambda_2}\right) \beta - 2y^\top X\beta + \lambda_1 \|\beta\|_1\right\}.
\tag{4}\]


Proof. By definition, \(\hat \beta^{\text{EN}}=(1+\lambda_2)\hat \beta^{\text{naive}}\). We introduce the transformation
\[
\beta = (1+ \lambda_2) b,
\]
where \(b\) represents the coefficient vector in the naive elastic net objective. Therefore,
\[
b = \frac{\beta}{1+\lambda_2}.
\]
Substituting this expression into the naive objective gives
\[
L(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, b) = \left\|y - X\frac{\beta}{1+\lambda_2} \right\|_2^2 + \lambda_2 \left\|\frac{\beta}{1+\lambda_2} \right\|_2^2 + \lambda_1 \left\|\frac{\beta}{1+\lambda_2} \right\|
\]
Expanding the squared-error term,
\[
L = y^\top y - \frac{2}{1+\lambda_2}y^\top X\beta + \frac{1}{(1+\lambda_2)^2} \beta^\top (X^\top X + \lambda_2 I)\beta + \frac{\lambda_1}{1+\lambda_2}\|\beta\|_1.
\]
Multiplying by the positive constant \(1 + \lambda_2\) does not change the mimizer. We obtain
\[
(1+\lambda_2) = (1+\lambda_2)y^\top y - 2y^\top X\beta + \beta^\top\left(\frac{X^\top X + \lambda_2 I}{1+\lambda_2}\right)\beta + \lambda_1 \|\beta\|_1
\]
The first term is independent of \(\beta\) can be omitted. The remaining expression is the objective in Equation 4.

Expanding the lasso objective and omitting \(y^\top y\) gives
\[
\hat \beta^{\text{lasso}} = \arg\min_\beta \{\beta^\top X^\top X\beta- 2y^\top X\beta + \lambda_1 \|\beta\|_1\}
\]
Both estimators contain the same linear term \(-2y^\top X \beta\) and the same \(L_1\)-penalty. Their difference lies entirely in the quadratic matrix. For the lasso, the quadratic term contains
\[
\hat \Sigma = X^\top X
\]
For the corrected elastic net, it contains
\[
\hat \Sigma_{\text{EN}} = \frac{X^\top X + \lambda_2 I}{1 + \lambda_2}
\]
Define
\[
\gamma = \frac{\lambda_2}{1+ \lambda_2}
\]
Then
\[
\hat \Sigma_{\text{EN}} = (1-\gamma)\hat \Sigma + \Sigma I.  
\]
This representation shows that the elastic net can be interpreted as a stabilized lasso, in which the Gram matrix is shrunk toward the identity matrix.
Because the predictor columns are standardized to have unit squared norm, the diagonal entries of \(\hat \Sigma\) equal one. Consequently,
\[
(\hat \Sigma_{EN})_{ii} = 1,
\]
while, for \(i \neq j\),
\[
(\hat \Sigma_{EN})_{ij} = \frac{\rho_{ij}}{1+ \lambda_2}
\]
The diagonal terms remain unchanged, while the off-diagonal correlations are reduced. The quadratic regularization therefore decreases the strength of predictor dependencies within the estimation problem.





flowchart TD
    A["Lasso quadratic matrix: XᵀX"]
    B["Add ridge stabilization: XᵀX + λ₂I"]
    C["Normalize by 1 + λ₂"]
    D["Diagonal entries remain 1"]
    E["Off-diagonal correlations shrink"]
    F["L1 penalty still permits sparsity"]
    G["Corrected elastic net"]
    A --> B
    B --> C
    C --> D
    C --> E
    D --> G
    E --> G
    F --> G






This also explains the connection with ridge regression’s treatment of correlated variables. Recall that the ridge estimator is
\[
\hat \beta^{\text{ridge}} = (X^\top X + \lambda_2 I)^{-1}X^\top y.
\]
Writing
\[
\hat \Sigma_{EN} = \frac{X^\top X + \lambda_2 I}{1 + \lambda_2},
\]
we can express the ridge operator as
\[
(X^\top X + \lambda_2 I)^{-1}X^\top  = \frac{1}{1+\lambda_2} \hat \Sigma_{\text{EN}}^{-1} X^\top.
\]
This decomposition separates ridge regression into two effects: stabilizing the Gram matrix and applying the shrink factor \(1/(1+\lambda_2)\). The corrected elastic net retains the first effect while eliminating the second through rescaling. Its remaining \(L_1\)-penalty provides both coefficient shrinkage and variable selection.
The stabilization also ensures uniqueness. Since \(\lambda_2 >0\),
\[
X^\top X + \lambda_2 I
\]
is positive definite. Therefore, the objective in Equation 4 is strictly convex in \(\beta\), and the corrected elastic net coefficient vector is unique even when \(X\) has linearly dependent columns.


5.3 The limiting connection to univariate soft thresholding
First, when \(\lambda_2 = 0\),
\[
\frac{X^\top X + \lambda_2 I}{1+\lambda_2 } = X^\top X.
\]
Equation 4 reduces to the ordinary lasso objective, so
\[
\hat \beta^{EN} (\lambda_1, 0) = \hat \beta^{\text{lasso}}(\lambda_1)
\]
At the other extreme, consider what happens when \(\lambda_2 \to \infty\), while \(\lambda_1\) remains fixed. We have
\[
\frac{X^\top X+\lambda_2 I}{1 + \lambda_2} \to I
\]
The limiting estimator therefore minimizes
\[
\hat \beta^{\infty} = \arg\min_{\beta} \{\beta^\top \beta - 2y^\top X \beta + \lambda_1 \|\beta\|_1\}
\tag{5}\]
Unlike the general lasso, this problem is separable across coordinates.

Proposition 7 (Univariate soft-thresholding limit) As \(\lambda_2\to \infty\), with \(\lambda_1\) fixed, the corrected elastic net coverges to
\[
\hat \beta_j^\infty = \mathrm{sign}(x_j^\top y) \left(|x_j^\top y| - \frac{\lambda_1}{2}\right)_{+}
\tag{6}\]


Proof. Expanding Equation 5,
\[
\beta^\top \beta - 2y^\top X \beta + \lambda_1 ||\beta||_1 = \sum_{j=1}^p [\beta_j^2 -2(x_j^\top y)\beta_j + \lambda_1 |\beta_j|]
\]
The coefficients can therefore be optimized independently. Writing \(z_j = x_j^\top y\), each coordinate minimizes
\[
\beta_j^2 -2z_j \beta_j + \lambda_1 |\beta_j|
\]
Completing the square produces
\[
(\beta_j- z_j)^2 + \lambda_1 |\beta_j|
\]
up to a constant. Applying the soft-thresholding theorem gives
\[
\hat \beta_j^\infty = S(z_j, \lambda_1 / 2),
\]
which is Equation 6.

This estimator is called univariate soft thresholding, since it thresholds each predictor’s marginal association with the response independently of the remaining predictors. At \(\lambda_2= 0\), the lasso uses the complete correlation structor of the predictor matrix. As \(\lambda_2\) increases, the off-diagonal elements of the effective Gram matrix decrease. In the limit, the objective behaves as though the predictors were orthogonal.


5.4 Computation and parameter selection for the elastic net
The augmented-data representation provides a direct computational strategy for the elastic net. For fixed \(\lambda_2\), one can solve the equivalent lasso problem in \(\beta^*\), then apply the rescaling in Definition 3. Zou and Hastie (2005) use this relationship to develop LARS-EN, an adaptation of least-angle regression that computes elastic net solution paths efficiently.
For a fixed active set \(A\) and sign vector \(s_A\), the naive elastic net first-order condition is
\[
2X_A^\top (X_A \hat \beta_A - y) + 2\lambda_2 \hat \beta_A + \lambda_1 s_A = 0
\]
Rearranging,
\[
2(X_A^\top X_A + \lambda_2 I) \hat \beta_A = 2X_A^\top y - \lambda_1 s_A.
\]
Therefore, \[
\hat \beta_A^\text{naive} = (X_A^\top X_A + \lambda_2 I)^{-1} \left(X_A^\top y - \frac{\lambda_1}{2}s_A \right)
\]
For fixed \(A\), \(s_A\), and \(\lambda_2\), this is an affine function of \(\lambda_1\). Consequently, just as in the lasso, the elastic net solution path is piecewise linear.
LARS-EN exploits this structure, updating the active set as the \(L_1\)-penalty changes. Rather than constructing all \(n+p\) rows of the augmented desgin matrix, the algorithm uses
\[
X_A^*\top X_A^* = \frac{X_A^\top X_A+\lambda_2 I}{1 + \lambda_2}
\]
and updates the relevant Cholesky factorizations as predictors enter or leave the model.
Coordinate descent provides another computational strategy. Holding all coefficients except \(\beta_j\) fixed, the naive elastic net coordinate problem is
\[
\min_{\beta_j} \{\|r_j - x_j \beta_j \|_2^2 + \lambda_2 \beta_j^2 + \lambda_1 \|\beta_j\|\}.
\]
The resulting exact coordinate update is
\[
\beta_j^\text{new} = \frac{S(x_j^\top r_j, \lambda_1/2)}{x_j^\top x_j + \lambda_2}
\]
Under the column normalization \(x_j^\top x_j = 1\),
\[
\beta_j^\text{new} = \frac{S(x_j^\top r_j, \lambda_1/2)}{1+\lambda_2}
\]
This resembles the lasso coordinate update, but incorporates an additional quadratic term in the denominator. After convergence, the original corrected elastic net is obtained by multiplying the naive coefficient vector by \(1+\lambda_2\).

title: Appendix A — OLS, Linear Invariance, and Conditional Independence
text:
1 Setup
This appendix expands the linear-model argument behind the conditional-independence result in Week 2. The goal is to separate the algebra from the main narrative, where the main point is conceptual: cross-validation can be a reasonable estimator of average prediction error while still being independent of the particular fitted model’s conditional prediction error.
Assume the homoscedastic Gaussian linear model
\[
\mathbf Y = \mathbf X\theta + \epsilon,
\qquad
\epsilon \mid \mathbf X \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I_n).
\tag{1}\]
Let \(\mathcal A\) be ordinary least squares. Conditional on \(\mathbf X\), the fitted parameter is
\[
\hat \theta
=
(\mathbf X^\top \mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top \mathbf Y
=
\theta + (\mathbf X^\top \mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top \epsilon.
\]
Thus, after conditioning on \(\mathbf X\), every source of randomness comes from the noise vector \(\epsilon\).
crumbs: A  OLS, Linear Invariance, and Conditional Independence

title: Appendix A — OLS, Linear Invariance, and Conditional Independence
text:
2 Geometry
OLS decomposes the response into a fitted component and a residual component:
\[
\mathbf Y
=
\underbrace{H\mathbf Y}_{\text{projection onto column space of } \mathbf X}
+
\underbrace{(I-H)\mathbf Y}_{\text{residual}},
\qquad
H = \mathbf X(\mathbf X^\top \mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top.
\]
Because \((I-H)\mathbf X\theta = 0\), the residual vector depends only on the noise:
\[
(I-H)\mathbf Y = (I-H)\epsilon.
\]
The fitted-model error, however, depends on the coefficient error
\[
\hat \theta - \theta
=
(\mathbf X^\top \mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top \epsilon.
\]
So the two quantities are driven by two different projections of the same Gaussian noise vector.





flowchart LR
    A["Gaussian noise epsilon"]
    B["Fitted-direction component X^T epsilon"]
    C["Residual component (I-H) epsilon"]
    D["Conditional prediction error Err_XY"]
    E["Linearly invariant estimator such as CV"]

    A --> B --> D
    A --> C --> E
crumbs: A  OLS, Linear Invariance, and Conditional Independence

title: Appendix A — OLS, Linear Invariance, and Conditional Independence
text:
3 Why linear invariance matters
A prediction-error estimator \(\widehat \Err\) is linearly invariant if adding any linear signal \(x_i^\top \kappa\) to every response does not change the estimator. In symbols,
\[
\widehat \Err((x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n, U)
=
\widehat \Err((x_i,y_i+x_i^\top\kappa)_{i=1}^n, U).
\]
For OLS with squared-error loss, cross-validation has this property. Adding \(x_i^\top\kappa\) shifts the fitted values in each training fold by the same linear signal. The held-out residuals are unchanged, so the squared held-out errors are unchanged.
Therefore, conditional on \(\mathbf X\), a linearly invariant estimator can depend on \(\mathbf Y\) only through residual information orthogonal to the column space of \(\mathbf X\):
\[
\widehat \Err = g((I-H)\epsilon, U)
\]
for some function \(g\).
crumbs: A  OLS, Linear Invariance, and Conditional Independence

title: Appendix A — OLS, Linear Invariance, and Conditional Independence
text:
4 Why the theorem follows
The conditional prediction error of the final OLS model depends on the fitted coefficient error, which is determined by \(\mathbf X^\top \epsilon\). A linearly invariant estimator such as OLS cross-validation depends on the residual component \((I-H)\epsilon\).
Under the Gaussian linear model, orthogonal projections of a Gaussian vector are independent. Since
\[
H\epsilon \perp\!\!\!\perp (I-H)\epsilon \mid \mathbf X,
\]
we get the key separation:
\[
\widehat \Err
\indep
\Err_{XY}
\mid
\mathbf X.
\]
This does not mean cross-validation is useless. It means that, in this setting, cross-validation is estimating a population-level or repeated-sample target more naturally than it is estimating the realized conditional error of the exact fitted model in hand.
crumbs: A  OLS, Linear Invariance, and Conditional Independence

title: Appendix B — Linear Algebra Review
text: 1 Vector spaces and their structures

title: Appendix B — Linear Algebra Review
text:
1.1 Vector spaces and subspaces

Definition 1 (Vector space) A set \(\mathcal V\) is a vector space if, for any \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}\in \mathcal V\) and scalars \(a, b\), operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication are defined such that

\((\mathbf u + \mathbf v) + \mathbf w = \mathbf u + (\mathbf v + \mathbf w)\)
\(\mathbf u + \mathbf v = \mathbf v + \mathbf u\)
There exists a vector \(\mathbf 0\in \mathcal V\) such that \(\mathbf u + \mathbf 0 = \mathbf u = \mathbf 0 + \mathbf u\) for any \(\mathbf u \in \mathcal V\).
For any \(\mathbf u \in \mathcal V\), there exists \(\mathbf w \equiv -u\) such that \(\mathbf u + \mathbf w = 0 = \mathbf w + \mathbf u\).
\(a (\mathbf u + \mathbf w) = a\mathbf u + a\mathbf w\).
\((a + b)\mathbf u = a\mathbf u + b \mathbf u\).
\((ab)\mathbf u = a(b\mathbf u)\).
There exists a scalar \(1\) such that \(1\mathbf u = \mathbf u\).


A standard example is \(\R^n=\{(x_1, \ldots, x_n)^\top: x_i \in \R\}\). A plane passing through the origin in \(\R^3\) is also a vector space under the usual operations.

Definition 2 (Subspace) Let \(\mathcal V\) be a vector space, and let \(\mathcal W\) be a set with \(\mathcal W\subset \mathcal V\). \(\mathcal W\) is a subspace of \(\mathcal V\) if \(\mathcal W\) is a vector space using the same definitions of vector addition and scalar multiplication as for \(\mathcal V\).


Theorem 1 (Subspace criterion) Let \(\mathcal V\) be a vector space, and let \(\mathcal W\) be a nonempty subset of \(\mathcal V\). If \(\mathcal W\) is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication, then \(\mathcal W\) is a subspace of \(\mathcal V\).

Equivalently, we need to verify \(\mathcal u, \mathcal v\in \mathcal W\implies u+v \in \mathcal W\) and \(a\in \R, \mathcal u\in \mathcal W \implies a\mathbf u \in \mathcal W\).

Proof. Since \(\mathcal W\) is nonempty, we can choose an arbitrary \(\mathbf w \in \mathcal W\). Closure under scalar multiplication implies \(\mathbf 0 \mathbf w = \mathbf 0 \in \mathcal W\). For any \(\mathbf u \in \mathcal W\), we also have \((-1)\mathbf u = -\mathbf u \in \mathcal W\). Thus the additive identity and additive inverses exist in \(\mathcal W\). The remanining vector-space axioms are inherited from \(\mathcal V\), since the addition and scalar multiplication operations are unchanged. Therefore \(\mathcal W\) is a vector space and hence a subspace.


Example 1 (Testing whether a set is a subspace) Consider \(W = \{(x, y, z)^\top \in \R^3: y = z\}\). If \(\mathcal u = (a, b, b)^\top\) and \(v=(c,d,d)^\top\), then
\[
u+ v = (a+ c, b+d, b+d)^\top \in W
\]
and
\[
\alpha u = (\alpha a, \alpha b, \alpha b)^\top \in W
\]
Hence \(W\) is a subspace of \(\R^3\).



1.2 Linear combinations, span, and linear independence

Definition 3 (Span) Given \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_r\in \mathcal V\), a linear combination is a vector of the form
\[
x = \sum_{i=1}^r a_i \mathbf v_i
\]
The set of all such linear combination is
\[
\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_r\} = \left\{\sum_{i=1}^r a_i\mathbf v_i: a_i\in \R \right\}
\]


Theorem 2 (Span is a subspace) The span of any finite collection of vectors in \(\mathcal V\) is a subspace of \(\mathcal V\).


Proof. Let \(\mathcal W=\mathrm{span}\{\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_r\}\). The zero vector belongs to \(\mathcal W\) by choosing every coefficient to be zero.
For arbitrary \(\mathbf x, \mathbf y \in \mathcal W\), we can write
\[
\mathbf x = \sum_{i=1}^r a_i \mathbf v_i, \quad \mathbf y = \sum_{i=1}^r b_i \mathbf v_i.
\]
Then
\[
\mathbf x + \mathbf y = \sum_{i=1}^r (a_i + b_i) \mathbf v_i \in \mathcal W
\]
Similarly, for any scalar \(c\),
\[
c\mathbf x = \sum_{i=1}^r (ca_i)\mathbf v_i \in \mathcal W.
\]
Theorem 1 establishes the result.


Definition 4 (Column space) For a matrix \(A\in \R^{n\times p}\) with columns \(a_1, \ldots, a_p\),
\[
\mathcal C(A) = \mathrm{span}\{a_1, \ldots, a_p\}= \{A\beta:\beta \in \R^p\}.
\]
Thus \(\mathcal C(A)\) is the collection of all vectors that can be obtained by multiplying \(A\) by a coefficient vector.

Some refer \(\mathcal C(A)\) as the range space of \(A\) and write it \(R(A)\). This concept is fundamental to linear models, because the possible fitted mean vectors of the model \(Y = X\beta + \epsilon\) lie in \(\mathcal C(X)\).

Definition 5 (Linear independence) Vectors \(\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_r\) are linear independent if
\[
\sum_{i=1}^ r a_i \mathbf v_i = \mathbf 0 \implies a_1 = \cdots = a_r = 0
\]
Otherwise, they are linearly dependent.

An equivalent characterization is that a collection is linearly dependent if one vector can be expressed as a linear combination of the others. For example,
\[
v_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{pmatrix}, \quad v_2 = \begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}, \quad v_3 = \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}
\]
are linearly dependent because \(v_3 = v_1 + v_2\).


1.3 Basis and dimension

Definition 6 (Basis) A collection \(\{\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_r\}\) is a basis for \(\mathcal V\) if it satisfies both conditions:

The vectors span \(\mathcal V\).
The vectors are linearly independent.


A basis therefore contains enough vectors to represent every vector in the space, without redundancy.

Theorem 3 (Invariance of basis size) Every basis of a finite-dimensional vector space contains the same number of vectors.


Proof. We use the following elementary consequence of linear independence, called the Steinitz exchange lemma:

If a collection of \(m\) vectors is linearly independent and another collection of \(n\) vectors spans the same space, then \(m\leq n\).

To establish this lemma, suppose \(\{u_1, \ldots, u_n\}\) spans the space and \(\{v_1, \ldots, v_m\}\) is linearly independent. We can express \(v_1\) as a combination of the \(u_i\). At least one coefficient is nonzero; therefore, one \(u_i\) can be solved for in terms of \(v_1\) and the remaining \(u_i\). Replacing that \(u_i\) with \(v_1\) preserves spanning.
Proceed inductively. Since the \(v_i\) are independent, each new \(v_i\) cannot lie in the span of the previously inserted \(v_j\). Consequently, another original \(u_i\) can be replaced while preserving spanning. We can perform at most \(n\) such replacements, so \(m\leq n\).
Now suppose \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) are two bases with \(r\) and \(s\) vectors, respectively. Because \(B_1\) is independent and \(B_2\) spans, \(r\leq s\). Reversing their roles gives \(r\geq s\). Therefore \(r=s\).


Definition 7 (Dimension and rank) The dimension of a vector space is the number of vectors in any basis. For a matrix \(A\),
\[
\rank(A) = \dim \mathcal C(A).
\]

Theorem 3 ensures that dimension and rank are well-defined, independent of the particular basis chosen.

Theorem 4 (Uniqueness of basis representation) If \(\{\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_r\}\) is a basis for \(\mathcal V\), every \(\mathbf x \in \V\) has a unique expression
\[
\mathbf x = \sum_{i=1}^r a_i \mathbf v_i
\]


Proof. Existence follows from the spanning property. For uniqueness, suppose
\[
\mathbf x = \sum_{i=1}^r a_i \mathbf v_i = \sum_{i=1}^r b_i \mathbf v_i.
\]
Subtracting, we have
\[
\mathbf 0 = \sum_{i=1}^r (a_i-b_i) \mathbf v_i \overset{\text{linear independence}}{\implies} a_i - b_i = 0 , \quad i=1,\ldots, r
\]
Therefore \(a_i = b_i\) for every \(i\).

Note that, a vector has unique coordinates relative to a basis, even though different bases produce different coordinate vectors.


1.4 Sums and direct sums of subspaces

Definition 8 (Sum of subspaces) For two subspaces \(\U, \W \subseteq \V\), define
\[
\U + \W = \{\mathbf u + \mathbf w: \mathbf u \in \U, \mathbf w\in \W\}.
\]
If additionally \(\U \cap \W = \{\mathbf 0\}\), the sum is called a direct sum, written \(\U \oplus \W\).

The intersection condition distinguishes a direct sum from a general sum.

Theorem 5 \(\U + \W\) is a subspace. Furthermore, if matrices \(A, B\) have the same number of rows,
\[
\mathcal C(\begin{bmatrix}A & B\end{bmatrix}) = \mathcal C(A) + \mathcal C(B)
\]


Proof. If \(x=u_1+ w_1\) and \(y = u_2+w_2\), then
\[
x+ y = (u_1 + u_2) + (w_1 + w_2) \in \U + \W.
\]
Also,
\[
cx = cu_1 + cw_1 \in \U + \W.
\]
Since \(\mathbf 0 \in \U + \W\), Theorem 1 shows that the sum is a subspace.
For the column-space identity, observe that every linear combination of columns of \(\begin{bmatrix}A & B \end{bmatrix}\) can be written
\[
\begin{bmatrix} A & B \end{bmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}a \\ b \end{pmatrix} = Aa + Bb.
\]
The first term belongs to \(\mathcal C\), and the second to \(\mathcal C(B)\). Conversely, every sum \(Aa + Bb\) is a linear combination of the concatenated columns. Hence the spaces coincide.


Theorem 6 (Uniqueness of direct-sum decomposition) If \(\U \cap \W = \{0\}\), then every \(x\in \U +\W\) has a unique decomposition
\[
x = u + w, \qquad u \in\U, w \in \W
\]


Proof. Suppose \(x = u_1+ w_1 = u_2 + w_2\). Rearranging gives \(u_1 - u_2 = w_2 - w_1\). The left side belongs to \(\U\), while the right side belongs to \(\W\). Therefore their common value lies in \(\U \cap \W = \{0\}\), giving \(u_1 = u_2, w_1 = w_2\). Thus the decomposition is unique.


Theorem 7 (Dimension of a direct sum) If \(\U \cap \W = \{0\}\), then \(\dim(\U + \W) =\dim\U + \dim\W\)


Proof. Let \(u_1, \ldots, u_r\) from a basis for \(\U\), and \(w_1, \ldots, w_s\) a basis for \(\W\). Their union spans \(\U + \W\).
To show linear independence, we assume
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{r} a_i u_i + \sum_{j=1}^{s} b_j w_j = 0.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^r a_i u_i = -\sum_{j=1}^s b_j w_j.
\]
The common vector belongs to \(U\cap W\), and is therefore zero. By independence of each original basis, all \(a_i\) and \(b_j\) must be zero. The union is a basis consisiting of \(r+ s\) vectors. Hence
\[
\dim(\U + \W) = r + s.
\]

A useful extension of Theorem 7 is
\[
\dim(\U + \W) = \dim \U + \dim \W - \dim(\U \cap \W).
\]

Proof. Choose a basis \(z_1, \ldots, z_k\) for \(\U \cap \W\). Extend it to bases
\[
(z_1, \ldots, z_k , u_1, \ldots, u_r)
\]
for \(\U\), and
\[
(z_1, \ldots, z_k, w_1, \ldots, w_s)
\]
for \(\W\). The combined collection \(z_1, \ldots, z_k, u_1, \ldots, u_r, w_1, \ldots, w_s\) spans \(\U+ \W\).
To prove indepedence, any zero linear combination can be rearranged so that a linear combination of the \(w_j\) belongs to \(\U \cap \W\). Independence of the extended basis of \(\W\) forces every coefficient to \(w_j\) to vanish.
Thus,
\[
\dim(\U + \W) = k+ r + s
\]
Since \(\dim\U = k + r\) and \(\dim \W = k+s\), the claimed formula follows.

2 Inner Products, Orthogonality, and Decompositions

2.1 Inner product and norm

Definition 9 (Euclidean inner product) For vectors \(x, y\in \R^n\),
\[
\langle x, y \rangle = x^\top y = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i.
\]
Their Euclidean norm is
\[
|| x|| = \sqrt{x^\top x}.
\]
Two vectors are orthogonal if \(x^\top y = 0\).
A collection \(\{q_1, \ldots, q_r\}\) is orthonomal if
\[
q_i^\top q_j =\begin{cases}1, & i = j, \\ 0, & i\neq j.\end{cases}
\]

Orthonomal bases are especially useful because coordinates can be computed using inner products:
\[
x = \sum_{i=1}^r (q_i^\top x)q_i \quad \text{for } x \in \mathrm{span}\{q_1, \ldots, q_r\}.
\]

Theorem 8 (The Gram-Schmidt Theorem) Every finite-dimensional inner-product space admits an orthonormal basis. More specifically, given a basis \(x_1, \ldots, x_r\), there exists an orthonomal basis \(q_1, \ldots, q_r\) satisfying
\[
\mathrm{span}\{q_1, \ldots, q_s\} = \mathrm{span}\{x_1, \ldots, x_s\}
\]
for \(s= 1, \ldots, r\).


Construction

Set \(w_1 = x_1\), \(q_1 = \frac{w_1}{||w_1||}\). For \(s=2,\ldots, r\), we define
\[
w_s = x_s - \sum_{i=1}^{s-1}(x_s^\top q_i)q_i
\]
and then \(q_s = \frac{w_s}{||w_s||}\).



Gram-Schmidt Orthonomal Basis



Proof. We proceed by induction on \(s\). For \(s=1\), since \(x_1 \neq 0\), \(q_1 = \frac{x_1}{||x_1||}\) is well-defined, satisfies \(||q_1|| = 1\), and spans the same space as \(x_1\).
Suppose \(q_1,\ldots, q_{s-1}\) are orthonomal and span precisely the space generated by \(x_1,\ldots, x_{s-1}\). We define
\[
w_s = x_s - \sum_{i=1}^{s-1} (x_s^\top q_i) q_i.
\]
For any \(j<s\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
    q_j^\top w_s &= q_j^\top x_s - \sum_{i=1}^{s-1} (x_s^\top q_i )q_j^\top q_i\\
    &= q_j^\top x_s - (x_s^\top q_j) \\
    &= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(w_s\) is orthogonal to all the previously constructed vectors.
Futhermore, \(w_s \neq 0\). Otherwise,
\[
x_s = \sum_{i=1}^{s-1}(x_s^\top q_i)q_i \in \mathrm{span}\{x_1, \ldots, x_{s-1}\}
\]
contradicting the linear independence of the original basis. Therefore \(q_s = \frac{w_s}{||w_s||}\) exists and has unit norm.
Finally, the construction shows that \(q_s\) lies in the span of \(x_1, \ldots, x_s\), while rearranging the formula for \(w_s\) expresses \(x_s\) in the span of \(q_1, \ldots, q_s\). Hence the two spans are equal at each step, and the complete collection is an orthonormal basis.



2.2 Orthogonal Complements

Definition 10 (Orthogonal complement) For a subspace \(\W\subseteq \V\), define
\[
W_V^{\perp} = \{x\in \V: x^\top w = 0 \quad \forall w \in \W\}
\]
When \(V= \R^{n}\), we write \(W^\perp\).


Corollary 1 (Trivial intersection) For any subspace \(\W\), \(\W \cap \W^\top = \{0\}\).


Proof. If \(x\in \W \cap \W^\top\), then \(x\in \W\) and \(x\) is orthogonal to every vector of \(\W\), including itself. Therefore
\[
x^\top x = || x||^2 = 0.
\]
Positive definiteness of the Euclidean inner product implies \(x=0\).


Theorem 9 (Orthogonal decomposition theorem) If \(\W \subseteq \V\), then \(\W_V^\perp\) is a subspace and
\[
\V = \W \oplus \W_V^\perp
\]


Proof. First, \(\W_V\) is a subspace. If \(x, y\in \W_{V}^\perp\) and \(a, b \in \R\), then for every \(w\in W\).
\[
(ax + by)^\top w = ax^\top w + by^\top w = 0.
\]
Thus \(ax + by \in \W_{V}^\perp\). Next, we select an orthonormal basis \(q_1, \ldots, q_r\) for \(\W\) using Gram-Schmidt. Extend this basis to an orthonormal basis
\[
q_1, \ldots, q_r, q_{r+1}, \ldots, q_n
\]
for \(V\), where \(n=\dim V\). Every \(x\in \V\) can therefore be written as
\[
x= \sum_{i=1}^n (x^\top q_i)q_i.
\]
Separate this into
\[
x = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^r (x^\top q_i) q_i}_{x_W} + \underbrace{\sum_{i=r+1}^n (x^\top q_i)q_i}_{x_\perp}
\]
Clearly \(x_W\in \W\). Because \(q_{r+1},\ldots, q_n\) are orthogonal to every vector in \(\W\), we have \(x_\perp \in \W_V^\perp\). Therefore \(\V = \W + \W_V^\perp\). By Corollary 1, their intersection is \(\{0\}\), so the sum is direct.


Corollary 2 (Unique orthogonal decomposition) Every \(x\in \V\) can be expressed uniquely as \(x=x_W + x_\perp\) where \(x_W \in \W\) and \(x_\perp \in W_V^{\perp}\). Moreover,
\[
\dim V = \dim W + \dim W_V^\top
\]




Orthogonal decomposition



Proof. Existence follows from Theorem 9, uniqueness from Theorem 6, and the dimension formula from Theorem 7.


Theorem 10 (Orthogonal complement of an intersection) For subspaces \(\U, \W \subseteq \R^n\),
\[
(\U \cap \W )^{\perp} = \U^\perp + \W^\perp
\]


Proof. We first establish two identities \((S^\perp)^\perp = S\), \((U+W)^\perp = U^\perp \cap W^\perp\). The first follows from orthogonal decomposition: if \(x\in (S^\perp)^\perp\), we can write \(x = s+ t\) with \(s\in S\), \(t\in S^\perp\). Since \(x\perp t\),
\[
0 = x^\top t = s^\top t + t^\top t = ||t||^2,
\]
so \(t=0\) and \(x=s \in S\).
For the second identity, a vector is orthogonal to every sum \(u+w\) when it is orthogonal to both \(U\) and \(W\). Applying this identity to \(U^\perp\) and \(W^\perp\),
\[
(U^\perp + W^\perp)^\perp = (U^\perp)^\perp \cap (W^\perp)^\perp = U\cap W.
\]
Taking orthogonal complements of both sides proves
\[
U^\perp + W^\perp = (U\cap W)^\perp
\]

This also establishes the two important identities:

\((U+ W)^\perp = U^\perp \cap W^\perp\) and
\((W^\perp)^\perp = W\).

3 Matrices and linear transfromations

3.1 Matrix operations and terminology



Concepts
Definition




Square matrix
\(A\in \R^{n\times n}\)


Transpose
\((A^\top)_{ij} = A_{ji}\)


Symmetric matrix
\(A= A^\top\)


Diagonal matrix
\(A_{ij} = 0\) for \(i\neq j\)


Identity matrix
\(I_n =\mathrm{diag}(1, \ldots, 1)\)


Nonsingular matrix
Square matrix possessing an inverse


Null space
\(\mathcal N(A) = \{x: Ax = 0\}\)



Matrix multiplication represents composition of linear transformations. If \(A: \R^p \to \R^n\), then
\[
T_A(x) = Ax
\]
is linear because
\[
A(ax + by) = aAx + bAy.
\]
The column space is the image of this transformation, whereas the null space is its kernel.


3.2 Matrix Invertibility

Theorem 11 (Invertibility and full rank) For \(A\in \R^{n\times n}\), the following are equivalent:
\[
A \text{ is nonsingular} \Longleftrightarrow \mathrm{rank}(A) = n
\]


Proof. Suppose \(A\) is nonsingular. If \(Ax = 0\), multiplying by \(A^{-1}\) gives
\[
x = A^{-1}Ax = A^{-1} 0 = 0.
\]
Thus the columns of \(A\) are linearly independent. Since there are \(n\) columns in \(\R^{n}\), they form a basis, so \(\mathrm{rank}(A) = n\).
Conversely, suppose \(\mathrm{rank}(A) = n\). THe columns of \(A\) form a basis for \(\R^{n}\). For each standard basis vector \(e_i\), there exists a unique vector \(b_i\) such that \(Ab_i = e_i\). We construct \(B= [b_1, \ldots, b_n]\). Then
\[
AB = [Ab_1, \ldots, Ab_n] = I.
\]
For every \(x\), \(A(BAx) = Ax\). Since \(A\) has linearly independnent columns, this implies \(BAx = x\). Hence \(BA = I\). Therefore \(B=A^{-1}\), and \(A\) is nonsingular.


Corollary 3 (Singularity and nontrivial null space) \(A_{n\times n}\) is singular if and only if there exists \(x\neq 0\) such that \(Ax = 0\).


Proof. By Theorem 11, \(A\) is singular when its columns are linearly dependent. Linear dependence means that there exists a nonzero coefficient vector \(x\) for which the linear combination of the columns vanishes, i.e. \(Ax = 0\).



3.3 Rank-nullity theorem

Theorem 12 (Rank-nullity theorem) If \(A\in \R^{m\times n}\), then \(\dim\mathcal N(A) +\mathrm{rank}(A) = n\).


Proof. Let \(k=\dim \mathcal N(A)\), and pick a basis \(v_1, \ldots, v_k\) for \(\mathcal N(A)\). Extend this basis to a basis for \(\R^n\):
\[
v_1, \ldots, v_k, w_1, \ldots, w_{n-k}.
\]
We claim that \(Aw_1, \ldots, Aw_{n-k}\) form a basis for \(\mathcal C(A)\). To establish spanning, take any \(y\in \mathcal C(A)\). Then \(y = Ax\) for some \(x\in \R^{n}\). Express \(x\) using the chosen basis:
\[
x = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i v_i + \sum_{j=1}^{n-k}b_j w_j.
\]
Applying \(A\), we have
\[
y = Ax = \sum_{j-1}^{n-k} b_j Aw_j,
\]
because \(Av_i = 0\). Thus the \(Aw_j\) span \(\mathcal C(A)\).
To establish independence, suppose
\[
\sum_{j-1}^{n-k} b_j Aw_j = 0.
\]
Then \(\sum_j b_j w_j \in \mathcal N(A)\), so it can be expressed as a combination of \(v_1, \ldots, v_k\). This gives a linear independence among the original basis vectors, unless every \(b_j = 0\). Hence the \(Aw_j\) are independent. Therefore, \(\mathrm{rank}(A) = n-k\), which establishes the theorem.

For \(A\in \R^{m\times n}\), the four fundamental subspaces satisfy
\[
\mathcal C(A), \mathcal N(A^\top) \subseteq \R^m, \quad \mathcal C(A^\top), \mathcal N(A)\subseteq \R^n
\]
Two orthogonality relationships are
\[
\mathcal C(A)^\perp = \mathcal N(A^\top) \quad \text{and} \quad \mathcal C(A^\top)^\perp = \mathcal N(A).
\]

Proof. For \(y\in \R^{m}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
y\in \mathcal C(A)^{\perp} &\Longleftrightarrow y^\top Ax = 0 \quad \forall x\in \R^{n}\\ &\Longleftrightarrow A^\top y = 0 \\ & \Longleftrightarrow y\in \mathcal N(A^\top).
\end{aligned}
\]
The second identity follows by replacing \(A\) with \(A^\top\).

Combining these identities with orthogonal decomposition gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\R^m = \mathcal C(A) \oplus \mathcal N(A^\top)\\
\R^n = \mathcal C(A^\top) \oplus \mathcal N(A).
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Appendix B — Linear Algebra Review
text:
4 Eigenvalues and Spectral Theory

4.1 Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

Definition 11 (Eigenvalue) For a square matrix \(A\), a scalar \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue if there exists a nonzero vector \(v\) such that
\[
Av = \lambda v.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
(A-\lambda I)v = 0,
\]
so \(A-\lambda I\) is singular.

The corresponding eigenspace is
\[
E_\lambda = \mathcal N(A-\lambda I).
\]
Its dimension is the geometric multiplicity of \(\lambda\).

Lemma 1 (Orthogonality of eigenvectors) If \(A\) is symmetric, eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.


Proof. Suppose \(Ax = \lambda x\), \(Ay = \mu y\), where \(\lambda \neq u\). Since \(A = A^\top\),
\[
x^\top Ay = (Ax)^\top y.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mu x^\top y = \lambda x^\top y \implies (\lambda - \mu) x^\top y =0.
\]
Because \(\lambda \neq \mu\), \(x^\top y = 0\).



4.2 Spectral Theorem

Theorem 13 (Eigenvector basis for the column space) If \(A\in \R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric, then \(\mathcal C(A)\) admits a basis consisting of eigenvectors corresponding to nonzero eigenvalues.


Proof. We establish the spectral decomposition by induction on the dimension. First, evey real symmetric matrix possesses a real eigenvector. One way to see this is to maximize the continuous function \(f(x) = x^\top Ax\) over the compact unit sphere \(\{x: ||x|| = 1\}\). At a maximizer \(u\), the Lagrange multiplier condition for the constraint \(u^\top u=1\) gives \(2Au = 2 \lambda u\), so \(Au = \lambda u\).
Now consider the orthogonal complement \(u^\perp\). For \(z\in u^\perp\),
\[
u^\top Az = (Au)^\top z = \lambda u^\top z = 0.
\]
Hence \(Az \in u^\perp\): the orthogonal complement is invariant under \(A\). The restriction of \(A\) to \(u^\perp\) remains symmetric. By induction, \(u^\perp\) has an orthonormal eigenbasis. Adjoining \(u\) gives an orthogonal eigenbasis \(q_1, \ldots, q_n\) for \(\R^n\).
Now we express any \(x\in \R^n\) as \(x = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i q_i\). Applying \(A\),
\[
Ax = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i \lambda_i q_i.
\]
Consequently, \(\mathcal C(A) = \mathrm{span}\{q_i: \lambda_i \neq 0.\}\).
Thus the nonzero-eigenvalue eigenvectors form a basis for the column space.


Theorem 14 Every real symmetric matrix \(A\) has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors for \(\R^n\).


Proof. By Theorem 13 and the orthogonal complement relation, \(\mathcal C(A)^\perp = \mathcal N(A)\) for symmetric \(A\), the eigenspaces associated with nonzero eigenvalues, together with the zero eigenspace, span \(\R^n\).
Apply Gram-Schmidt within each eigenspace to produce an orthonormal basis there. Every linear combination of eigenvectors with the same eigenvalue remains an eigenvector for that eigenvalue. Eigenvectors from distinct eigenspaces are automatically orthogonal, by the previous Lemma 1. Combining these orthonormal bases therefore produces an orthonormal eigenbasis of \(\R^n\).



4.3 Orthogonal matrices and diagonalization

Definition 12 A square matrix \(Q\) is orthogonal if \(Q^\top Q = QQ^\top = I\). Equivalently, \(Q^{-1} = Q^\top\).


Theorem 15 \(Q\in \R^{n\times n}\) is orthogonal if and only if its columns form an orthonormal basis for \(\R^n\).


Proof. Write \(Q = [q_1, \ldots, q_n]\). The \((i, j)\)-entry of \(Q^\top Q\) is \(q_i^\top q_j\). Therefore \[
Q^\top Q = I \Longleftrightarrow q_i^\top q_j = \delta_{ij}
\]
This means the columns are orthonormal. Since there are \(n\) independent columns in \(\R^n\), they form a basis.
Conversely, an orthonormal basis gives \(Q^\top Q = I\). Because \(Q\) is square, this implies \(Q^{-1} = Q^\top\).


Corollary 4 (Characterization by rows) \(Q\) is orthogonal if and only if its rows form an orthonomal basis.


Proof. Q is orthogonal if and only if \(Q^\top\) is orthogonal. Apply Theorem 15 to \(Q^\top\).


Theorem 16 (For every real symmetric matrix \(A\), there exists an orthogonal matrix \(Q\) such that) \[
Q^\top A Q = \Lambda, \quad \Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n).
\]


Proof. By Theorem 14, we choose an orthonomal eigenbasis \(q_1, \ldots, q_n\), satisfying \(Aq_i = \lambda_i q_i\). Let \(Q= [q_1,\ldots, q_n]\). Then
\[
AQ = [\lambda_1q_1, \ldots, \lambda_nq_n]= Q\Lambda.
\]
Multiplying by \(Q^\top\) yields
\[
Q^\top AQ = Q^\top Q\Lambda = \Lambda
\]


Corollary 5 Because \(QQ^\top = I\),
\[
A=Q\Lambda Q^\top = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i q_i q_i^\top .
\]


Proof. Multiply the identity \(Q^\top A Q = \Lambda\) on the left by \(Q\) and on the right by \(Q^\top\). Expanding the product by columns gives the summation.




Orthogonal diagonalization


Note that eigenvalues determine the scaling, whereas eigenvectors determine the direction.


4.4 Positive definite and positive semidefinite matrices

Definition 13 (Postive definite) A real symmetric matrix \(A\) is positive definite if
\[
x^\top Ax > 0 \quad \forall x\neq 0
\]
It is positive semidefinite (called nonnegative) if
\[
x^\top A x \geq 0 \quad \forall x
\]


Theorem 17 (Eigenvalue characterization) For symmetric \(A\),
\[
A \succeq 0 \Longleftrightarrow \lambda_i \geq 0 \quad \forall i
\]
and
\[
A \succ 0 \Longleftrightarrow \lambda_i > 0 \quad \forall i
\]


Proof. Using the spectral decomposition, let \(z = Q^\top x\). Then
\[
x^\top Ax = z^\top \Lambda z = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i z_i^2.
\]
If every eigenvalue is nonnegative, every summand is nonnegative. Conversely, if \(\lambda_j < 0\), choosing \(x = q_j\) gives \(x^\top A x = \lambda_j < 0\), contradicting positive semidefiniteness.
Similarly, all eigenvalues being strictly positive makes the quadratic form strictly positive for every nonzero \(x\), and a nonpositive eigenvalues contradicts positive definiteness.


Theorem 18 (Factorization of positive semidefinite matrices) For symmetric \(A\),
\[
A\succeq 0 \Longleftrightarrow \exists B \in \R^{n\times n}: A = BB^\top
\]


Proof. If \(A \succeq 0\), every eigenvalue is nonnegative. We define \(B = Q\,\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_1}, \ldots, \sqrt{\lambda_n})\). Then
\[
BB^\top = Q\, \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n) Q^\top = A.
\]
Conversely, if \(A = BB^\top\), then for every \(x\),
\[
x^\top Ax = x^\top BB^\top x = ||B^\top x||^2 \geq 0
\]
Hence \(A \succeq 0\).


Corollary 6 (Positive definiteness and nonsingularity) If \(A=BB^\top\), then
\[
A\succ 0 \Longleftrightarrow B \text{ is nonsingular}.
\]


Proof. For every nonzero \(x\), \(x^\top Ax = ||B^\top x||^2\). This is strictly positive for every \(x\neq 0\) when \(\mathcal N(B^\top)=\{0\}\). Since \(B\) is square, this is equivalent to nonsigularity of \(B\).

For any \(X \in \R^{n\times p}\), \(X^\top X \succeq 0\) since \(\beta^\top X^\top X \beta=||X\beta||^2 \geq 0\). Moreover,
\[
X^\top X \succ 0 \Longleftrightarrow \mathrm{rank}(X) = p.
\]

title: Appendix B — Linear Algebra Review
text:
5 Orthogonal projections

5.1 Orthogonal projection operators

Definition 14 Let \(W = \mathcal C(X) \in \R^n\). A matrix \(P\in \R^{n\times n}\) is the orthogonal projection matrix onto \(W\) if
\[
\begin{aligned}
Pv = v &\quad\forall v\in W\\
Pw = 0 & \quad \forall w\in W^\perp
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, for the unique decomposition \(y = y_W + y_\perp\), the projection satisfies
\[
Py = y_W, \quad (I-P)y = y_\perp
\]


Proposition 1 (Column space of a projection) If \(P\) is the orthogonal projection onto \(\mathcal C(X)\), then \(\mathcal C(P) = \mathcal C(X)\).


Proof. For any \(y = y_W + y_\perp\), \(Py = y_W \in \mathcal C(X)\). Therefore \(\mathcal C(P) \subseteq \mathcal C(X)\).
Conversely, for every \(v \in \mathcal C(X)\), \(Pv = v\), so \(v\in \mathcal C(P)\). Thus \(\mathcal C(X) \subseteq \mathcal C(P)\).



5.2 Characterization of orthogonal projections

Theorem 19 A square matrix \(P\) is an orthogonal projection onto its column space if and only if
\[
P^2 = P, \qquad P^\top = P.
\]


Proof. Suppose \(P\) is an orthogonal projection. For every \(x\), we write \(x= u+ v\) with \(u\in \mathcal C(P)\) and \(v \in \mathcal C(P)^\perp\). Then
\[
P^2X = P(Px) = Pu = u = Px.
\]
Hence \(P^2 = P\). For symmetry, let take arbitrary vectors \(x = x_W + x_\perp\) and \(y = y_W+ y_\perp\). We have
\[
x^\top Py = (x_W + x_\perp)^\top y_W = x_W^\top y_W.
\]
Similarly,
\[
(Px)^\top y = x_W^\top (y_W + y_\perp) = x_W^\top y_W
\]
Therefore \(x^\top P y = x^\top P^\top y\) for all \(x, y\), which implies \(P= P^\top\).
Now suppose \(P^2 = P\) and \(P= P^\top\). For \(v\in \mathcal C(P)\), we write \(v = Px\). Then
\[
Pv = P^2x = Px = v.
\]
For \(w\perp \mathcal C(P)\), \(P^\top w = 0\) because every column of \(P\) is orthogonal to \(w\). By symmetry, \(Pw = 0\). Therefore \(P\) satisfies the defining properties of an orthogonal projection.


Proposition 2 (Uniqueness) The orthogonal projection onto a specified subspace is unique.


Proof. Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be orthogonal projections onto \(W\). For arbitrary \(x\), we can write \(x = x_W + x_\perp\). Then \(Px = x_W = Qx\). Since this equality holds for every \(x\), \(P = Q\).



5.3 Construction using an orthonormal basis

Theorem 20 If the columns of \(Q \in \R^{n\times r}\) form an orthonormal basis for \(W\), then
\[
P_W = QQ^\top = \sum_{i=1}^r q_i q_i^\top.
\]


Proof. Since \(Q^\top Q = I_r\),
\[
P_W^2 = QQ^\top QQ^\top = Q(Q^\top Q)Q^\top = QQ^\top = P_W
\] Also,
\[
P_W^\top = (QQ^\top)^\top = QQ^\top
\]
Thus \(P_W\) is symmetric and idempotent.
Moreover, \(\mathcal C(P_W) = \mathcal C(Q) = W\), one inclusion follows because every column of \(QQ^\top\) belongs to \(\mathcal C(Q)\), and the reverse follows from \(P_W Q = QQ^\top Q = Q\). By Theorem 19, \(QQ^\top\) is the orthogonal projection onto \(W\).


Example 2 (Projection onto a line) Consider the line \(W = \mathrm{span}\{\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}\}\). An orthonormal basis is the single vector \(q = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Hence
\[
P_W = qq^\top =\frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix}4&2 \\ 2&1\end{pmatrix}
\]
For \(y = (3,4)^\top\),
\[
P_W y = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix}4&2 \\ 2&1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}3\\4\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}4\\2 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The residual is \(y-P_W y = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}\)
We can check for it orthogonality: \(\begin{pmatrix} 4& 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}=0\)




Orthogonal projection example




5.4 Least squares as orthogonal projection
Suppose we want to minimize \(L(\beta) = ||y-X\beta||^2\). A minimizing fitted vector \(\hat y = \mathbf X\hat \beta\) must be the projection of \(y\) onto \(\mathcal C(X)\).
